analysis.one_liner: Lets workers opt to shift part of their Social Security taxes into personal investment accounts, paid for by cutting future guaranteed benefits.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the last weeks of 2000 with zero cosponsors, the bill died in the Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or vote when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let workers born after 1945 ask the Social Security Administration to open a personal account, into which the government would move up to 3.5% of their wages from the Social Security trust fund. The money would be invested much like the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, and paid out at retirement as an annuity or equal yearly installments. To make the math work, the bill would have changed how initial benefits are calculated, switching from wage-based to price-based indexing, which would lower promised benefits for every future retiree, and would have let the trust funds borrow from the Treasury up to the value of those cuts.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers born after 1945 who opt in would own a bequeathable account credited with a share of their wages, keeping investment gains beyond the reduced guaranteed benefit. Disabled beneficiaries could draw their account balance in monthly installments. The annuity and asset-management world would gain a large stream of accounts whose payouts must, by default, be converted into annuities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Opt-in workers and the annuity industry

how_it_helps.text: Eligible workers who submit a written request get a personal account credited annually with a percentage of their wages — up to 3.5%, scaled down for higher earners — transferred from the Social Security trust fund [S3].

Accounts are invested under the same rules as the federal Thrift Savings Plan, with fiduciary duties, periodic statements, and protection against being assigned or seized, and balances pass to a surviving spouse or estate if the holder dies [S3].

At retirement, holders choose equal annual installments over their life expectancy or an immediate annuity; balances of $3,500 or less are paid as a single lump sum, and disability beneficiaries can draw monthly installments while entitled [S3].
The bill's Title II is framed as a solvency fix, changing benefit indexing and adding trust-fund borrowing authority to keep the rest of the program funded [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Every future retiree pays, whether or not they open an account: the bill replaces wage-based indexing of initial benefits with slower price-based indexing, which compounds into substantially lower monthly checks over a career. The trust funds also lose the diverted payroll revenue and would borrow from the Treasury's general fund up to the present value of the benefit cuts, creating explicit federal debt. Account holders who opt in bear investment losses directly, since net losses are allocated pro rata to their accounts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Future retirees and the trust funds

drawbacks.text: The price-indexing change in Section 201 applies to everyone born after December 31, 1945 who becomes entitled to or dies before entitlement after 2002, lowering initial old-age and disability benefits regardless of whether the person ever opened an account [S3].

Benefits are additionally reduced by 1/36 of a percent for every month between the first transfer into a person's account and their entitlement to benefits, so participants trade a guaranteed monthly check for market exposure [S3].
Net investment losses are allocated pro rata to individual accounts, meaning workers who retire after a downturn would see their balances — and lifetime income — drop [S3].

Section 203 lets the trust funds borrow from the general fund of the Treasury up to the discounted present value of the future benefit reductions, converting the transition into explicit federal borrowing through 2050 [S3].

A good-faith supporter would have to acknowledge the transition gap: diverting up to 3.5% of wages out of the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund while current benefits still must be paid leaves a hole filled only by the new borrowing authority [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The account side is conservatively designed — government-run, low-fee investment in the Thrift Savings Plan mold, mandatory annuitization, small balances paid in cash — which limits both the upside and the fee skimming critics usually cite. But the financing is the problem: the same bill quietly cuts the guaranteed benefit for all future retirees through price indexing, whether they opt in or not, and covers the transition with Treasury borrowing. Workers would own a riskier benefit on top of a smaller guaranteed one; it is a real trade-off, and the bill never explains the cut in plain terms.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on December 14, 2000, and sat there untouched until the Congress ended three weeks later, so it never got a hearing, a vote, or even a cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. John Kasich introduced the Personal Social Security Account Act of 2000 in the House on December 14, 2000, in the final session days of the 106th Congress [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which was the only action the bill ever received [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor — the cosponsor count was zero [S4].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and all bills not passed died with it; this bill never left committee, so no vote was ever held [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any action, nothing changed: guaranteed Social Security benefits, calculated under wage indexing, were left intact for future retirees, and the annuity and asset-management industry gained no new mandated market. With zero cosponsors, not even the sponsor's own party advanced it.

for.name: Rep. John Kasich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 14, 2000 and delivered introductory remarks; it was his sole cosponsorless effort at the end of the Congress [S1][S5].

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over Social Security legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 14, 2000 and took no further action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: House members of both parties
against.role: 435 House members who could have cosponsored

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only measurable signal is a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: Account balances at retirement must by default be paid as an immediate annuity or equal installments over life expectancy, with lump sums limited to $3,500 or less, creating a large mandated annuity market for insurers [S3]. The requirement protects retirees from outliving their savings, but it channels payouts through insurers rather than leaving the choice with the account holder.

The accounts would be invested under the Thrift Savings Plan model — government-run, index-based, low-fee — so management fees are limited by design [S3]. The industry would gain a new pool of payroll-funded assets, but far less fee revenue than under a private-accounts plan run through commercial fund managers.

Up to 3.5% of each worker's wages would be transferred out of the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, and the program's promised benefits would be cut through price-based indexing of initial benefits, with any shortfall covered by borrowing from the Treasury [S3].
